claims.text: Solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn has an intrinsic, optimized strength–ductility balance.
The dynamic mechanical response of solidified FeNiCrMn depends systematically on temperature and strain rate.
The dynamic response of FeNiCrMn is governed by a transition between dislocation-mediated plasticity and deformation twinning or a rapid phase transformation.
Dislocation slip is the dominant deformation mechanism in FeNiCrMn at higher temperatures and lower strain rates.
Deformation twinning or a rapid phase transformation becomes dominant in FeNiCrMn at lower temperatures and higher strain rates.
Lower temperature and higher strain rate reduce dislocation mobility in FeNiCrMn.
Reduced dislocation mobility activates deformation twinning or a rapid phase transformation.
Twinning or transformation increases the flow strength of FeNiCrMn.
Twinning or transformation accommodates plastic strain in FeNiCrMn.
The mechanism transition preserves the alloy's strength–ductility balance.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate loading will produce higher yield strength than high-temperature, low-strain-rate loading.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate specimens will contain microstructural evidence of twinning or transformation.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate specimens will exhibit predominantly dislocation slip without pronounced twinning.
Ductility will remain similar between the high-temperature/low-rate and low-temperature/high-rate regimes.
Processing or compositional changes that introduce substantial microstructural heterogeneity may invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Extreme loading conditions may introduce adiabatic shear banding as an alternative failure mechanism.
